title: Stage 8 Maths: The Tests and How to Prepare
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Start here
summary: How Stage 8 maths is tested, how the two papers and the mark scheme work, what Thinking and Working Mathematically means, and how to use this course.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: This course covers the whole Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics Stage 8 curriculum (curriculum framework 0862).
Number: integers, powers and roots; place value and rounding; fractions, decimals, percentages, ratio and proportion.
Algebra: expressions, equations and formulae; sequences, functions and graphs.
Geometry and measure: shapes and measurements; position and transformation.
Statistics and probability: collecting, showing and comparing data; probability.
Thinking and Working Mathematically (TWM.01–TWM.08) runs through every strand.

blocks.text: Written by Mohamed Abdelkriem for students in British and international schools and their parents. Read this page first: it explains the tests you will sit, how they are marked, and how to use the rest of the course.
Which test, and when?

The **Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint** test in mathematics is taken at the **end of Stage 9**, not Stage 8. Since 2023 the Checkpoint test assesses the final stage only (Stage 9). It is set and marked by Cambridge, and the subject code is **0862**. Stage 9 work builds directly on what you learn in Stage 8, so a strong Stage 8 year is the foundation for a good Checkpoint result.

In Stage 8 your **school** tests you, usually at the end of the year. Cambridge provides **Lower Secondary Progression Tests** for Stage 8 that schools can use: they are classroom tests, **marked by your teachers in school**, and they can be used at any time in the year. Your school may use them or write its own tests in the same style. **This course prepares you for Stage 8 end-of-year tests in the Progression Test and Checkpoint style, and builds the base for Checkpoint in Stage 9.**

blocks.text: The two papers

The Stage 8 Progression Tests and the Stage 9 Checkpoint test have the same shape: **two papers, each 1 hour long and worth 50 marks**. Paper 1 is **non-calculator**; on Paper 2 you **may use a calculator**.

blocks.text: 50 marks in 60 minutes is about **72 seconds per mark** (3600 ÷ 50 = 72). A [1] question should take about a minute; a [3] question about three or four minutes. If you are stuck, move on and come back.
What the cover tells you

items: **Answer all questions.** There is no choice, so never leave a space empty — a sensible attempt can earn part marks.
**Write your answer in the space provided.** Answers go on the answer line, often with the unit already printed after it (cm, kg, E£…).
**Show all your working.** Working can earn marks even when the final answer is wrong.
**Marks are shown in brackets [ ].** [2] usually means two steps or two things to write.

**Pen and pencil.** Checkpoint papers ask for a black or dark blue pen, with an HB pencil allowed for diagrams and graphs, and no erasable pen or correction fluid. Follow the instructions on your own school's paper.

blocks.text: Question styles you will meet

Recent papers have had **no multiple-choice section**. All questions are short-answer or structured questions written on the paper, often with parts (a), (b), (c) about one context. The styles below appear again and again — every lesson page in this course practises them.

rows: Show each step. Simplify the answer if the question asks.
"Draw a ring around the best estimate."
Ring exactly one answer unless told otherwise.
"Is Ali correct? Tick a box and explain."
The tick alone rarely scores — the explanation or example earns the mark.
a table of values, a two-way table, a missing number
Check that each row follows the rule.
plot a graph, enlarge a shape, draw a frequency diagram
Use a sharp pencil and a ruler; plot points exactly.
angles and lengths you must calculate
Never measure a diagram that says NOT TO SCALE — calculate.
expand, factorise, solve, make x the subject
Write every step that leads to the given answer.

blocks.text: Understanding the mark scheme

Teachers (for Progression Tests) and Cambridge examiners (for Checkpoint) mark with a **mark scheme** that has five columns: **Question, Answer, Marks, Part marks, Guidance**. These short words appear in the Guidance column. Knowing them shows you how to collect every mark.

rows: Any correct equivalent answer scores, e.g. 3/5, 6/10 or 0.6 — unless the question says "simplest form" or "as a decimal".
Only the exact answer scores. Check your final form and sign carefully.
If part (a) is wrong but you use your wrong answer correctly in part (b), you can still get the mark for (b). Always attempt the next part!
Once a correct answer is seen, extra harmless working after it is ignored.
A step can earn a mark if it is written down or clearly used.
A correct answer reached by a wrong method does not score.
A mark given for a particular common partial answer.
extra information that is not required but may be given
You do not need to write it, but writing it is not penalised.
marks for a correct step, e.g. "1 mark for 24 seen"
This is why you show your working: a correct step still scores.

blocks.text: Worked examples: how marks are given
**Worked example 1** — part marks for working. Question: Work out 15% of 240. [2]

rows: Correct method seen (part mark), but an addition slip.
Wrong answer and no working to give a part mark.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — follow through. Question: (a) A pen costs E£12. Work out the cost of 7 pens. [1] (b) Omar pays for the 7 pens with a E£100 note. Work out his change. [1]

items: Suppose a student writes (a) 74 (wrong). In (b) they write 100 − 74 = 26. Part (b) still earns **1 mark (FT)** because the method used their own answer correctly.
Lesson: never skip part (b) because you are unsure of part (a).

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — or equivalent. Question: Write 0.6 as a fraction. [1] Answers 6/10 and 3/5 both score (oe). But if the question said **"in its simplest form"**, only 3/5 would score.

blocks.title: Exam technique for both papers
items: Read the whole question, then underline the instruction words: simplest form, nearest whole number, to 2 significant figures, show your working.
Write the unit if the answer line does not print it.
On Paper 1, set out written methods neatly — long multiplication, division and fraction work all carry part marks.
On Paper 2, write down what you type into the calculator, and estimate first so you notice typing slips.
Check that the answer makes sense: a probability is between 0 and 1; an angle in a triangle is less than 180°; a discount makes the price smaller.
Use any time left to re-check the questions you were least sure of.

blocks.text: How results are reported

**Progression Tests** are marked by teachers in school. Cambridge gives guidance on what percentage of the marks matches each performance band. For the 2023/2024 Lower Secondary mathematics Progression Tests the minimum indicative percentages were:
**Checkpoint (end of Stage 9)** is marked by Cambridge. Raw marks are converted to a **Checkpoint score from 0 to 50**, reported for the subject and for each strand. The same bands are used:

Cambridge says that "Good" is about an IGCSE grade C/4 on average and "Outstanding" is about A/7. From 2026 Checkpoint is offered in three series — **March, May and October** — on dates fixed by Cambridge. A missed Checkpoint test cannot be taken on another day.

blocks.title: For parents
blocks.text: Ask the school which tests your child will sit in Stage 8 and when. Results by strand (Number, Algebra, Geometry and measure, Statistics and probability) show exactly which section of this course to revise. A child who can do the practice quiz on every page without help is well prepared for Stage 8 tests and well placed for Checkpoint in Stage 9.
Thinking and Working Mathematically (TWM)

TWM is not a separate topic. It describes **how** a mathematician thinks, and the curriculum builds it into every strand, so it appears inside ordinary questions. There are eight characteristics, in four pairs:

rows: Choosing an example and checking whether it fits a rule
Testing "n^{2} + n + 1 is always prime" with n = 4: 21 = 3 × 7, so it fails.
Spotting a pattern that many examples share and stating the rule
Seeing that every product of two negative numbers is positive.
Making a mathematical guess or asking a question
"I think the exterior angle of a triangle equals the two opposite interior angles added."
Giving evidence to justify or challenge an idea
"Ali is wrong: the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, not 4 × 6 = 24."
Describing the mathematical properties of an object
"A rhombus has four equal sides and its diagonals cross at right angles."
Sorting objects into groups by their properties
Sorting numbers into natural numbers, integers and rational numbers.
Comparing methods or representations and judging their strengths and weaknesses
Deciding whether a pie chart or a bar chart shows the data better.
Refining a method to make it better or more efficient
Replacing listing multiples with a Venn diagram of prime factors to find an LCM.

blocks.text: In tests, TWM appears as words like **"Explain", "Show that", "Is she correct?", "Give an example", "Which method is better and why?"**. One clear counter-example is enough to show that a statement is false; to show that something is always true you need a reason, not just examples.

blocks.text: How to use this course

The course follows the Stage 8 curriculum strand by strand. Every lesson page has the objectives with their codes, key words with Arabic meanings, diagrams, worked examples in test style, common mistakes, exam tips and an interactive practice quiz with full solutions. At the end there are three full practice tests in the two-paper format.

rows: Order of operations and integers; factors, primes, HCF and LCM; types of number and index laws; squares, cubes and roots; multiplying and dividing by 0.1 and 0.01 and significant figures; fractions; percentages; decimals; ratio and proportion
Expressions; formulae; equations and inequalities; sequences; functions and straight-line graphs; real-life graphs
Quadrilaterals and polygons; circumference and miles/kilometres; area; 3D shapes; volume and surface area; angles; constructions; bearings and midpoints; transformations
Data collection and sampling; representing data; averages and comparing distributions; probability
Full Paper 1 + Paper 2 style tests with solutions

blocks.text: **For each lesson page:**

items: Read the "In the curriculum" box so you know the goal.
Copy the key words and rules into your notebook.
Cover each worked example, try it yourself, then compare your working line by line.
Do the practice quiz without help (no calculator unless the quiz says so), then read every solution — even for the ones you got right.
Write down your mistakes and redo those questions a week later.

blocks.text: **A suggested year plan:** work through about one lesson page a week in the order of the course (Number in the first term, Algebra and the first Geometry pages in the second, the rest of Geometry and Statistics and probability in the third). In the last three or four weeks before your end-of-year tests, do the three practice tests under timed conditions — 1 hour per paper — and revise the pages where you lost the most marks.

blocks.title: Common mistakes in maths tests
items: Writing only the final answer on a [2] or [3] question — no working means no part marks.
Measuring a diagram marked NOT TO SCALE instead of calculating.
Ignoring the instruction: "simplest form", "to 1 decimal place", "in index form".
Leaving out units or writing the wrong unit (cm instead of cm^{2}).
Answering "Yes" or "No" to an "Is he correct?" question with no reason or example.
Skipping part (b) because part (a) went wrong — follow-through marks are lost.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks questions
items: Questions often start with a context (a shop, a journey, a survey) and then ask parts (a), (b), (c). Information in the stem is needed in later parts.
The number of marks tells you how much to write: [1] = one answer; [2] = a method step and an answer, or two facts.
"Show your working" means the answer alone may not get full marks.
Paper 1 tests mental and written methods, so practise them without a calculator; on Paper 2 a calculator is allowed, but you still need to show the method you used.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Stage 8 maths tests: quick quiz
blocks.intro: Eight quick questions about the tests, the mark scheme and Thinking and Working Mathematically.

questions.q: How long is each paper in the Stage 8 Progression Tests and in Checkpoint mathematics?
On which paper are you NOT allowed to use a calculator?
questions.e: Paper 1 is non-calculator. A calculator may be used on Paper 2.

questions.q: How many marks is each paper worth?
questions.e: Each paper is worth 50 marks, so there are 100 marks in total.

questions.q: The Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint mathematics test assesses which stage?
questions.e: Since 2023 Checkpoint assesses the final stage only, Stage 9. Stage 8 is tested by your school, for example with Progression Tests.

questions.q: In a mark scheme, what does "FT" mean?
questions.e: FT means follow through: if you use your own wrong answer from an earlier part correctly, you can still earn the later mark.

questions.q: Which TWM characteristic means "choosing an example and checking whether it fits a rule"?
questions.e: Specialising is choosing a particular example and testing it against the rule. Its partner, generalising, is finding the rule that many examples share.

questions.q: Sara says, "All prime numbers are odd." Write the number that shows Sara is wrong.
questions.e: 2 is a prime number (its only factors are 1 and 2) and it is even. One counter-example is enough to show a statement is false — this is convincing.

questions.q: Explain why you should always show your working, even when you think your answer is correct.
questions.ms: 1 mark: working can earn part marks if the final answer is wrong / a correct step can score. 1 mark: any one other valid reason, e.g. some questions say "show your working" and the answer alone may not get full marks; follow-through marks in later parts depend on seeing your method; it helps you check your answer.
questions.e: Mark schemes give part marks for correct steps (e.g. "1 mark for 24 seen"), so working can still score if you make a slip at the end. Some questions say "show your working", so an answer alone may not get full marks, and follow-through marks depend on the examiner seeing your method.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Stage 8: school tests, for example with Progression Tests. Checkpoint: end of Stage 9, set and marked by Cambridge.
Two papers, 1 hour and 50 marks each. Paper 1: no calculator. Paper 2: calculator allowed.
Answer every question on the paper and show your working — part marks and follow-through marks depend on it.
Know the mark-scheme words: oe, cao, FT, isw, soi, nfww, SC.
TWM is in every topic: specialise and generalise, conjecture and convince, characterise and classify, critique and improve.
